e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “do good”: it describes carrying out an action that benefits others or accords with what is good. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it appears three times, so its basic meaning is clear even though it is not common in this corpus. The exact force of the action depends on the sentence where it occurs, but the central idea remains actively doing what is good.

This word is the proper name “Aleph,” also rendered “Alef.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs one time, in Joshua 19:25. The word’s specific role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here. Its lexical sense remains the name Aleph within this LXX corpus.

This word means “registering”: the act of entering or recording something in a register or written list. As a noun, it names the process rather than describing an action addressed to someone. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 2:13; the available lexical meaning is “registering.” The precise force of the noun in that passage depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

This verb means “dry up”: to lose moisture or become dry. It describes the action or process by which something wet or flowing becomes dry. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, across Jeremiah, Hosea, and Sirach. The word itself expresses drying rather than merely being dry, so it points to a change of condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is said to be drying up.

This Greek LXX verb means “requite to” or “repay to,” describing an action of returning something in response to what another person has done. It functions as a verb, so it expresses the act of repaying rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 24:20. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the action being described.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “cleanse” or “purge”: to remove what makes something unclean and bring it into a clean state. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek text of the Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 25:4. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular force of the word there, but its basic sense is the act of cleansing or purifying.

This Greek LXX verb means “wash away”: to remove something by washing or by the force of flowing water. It describes an action rather than an object, so it answers what someone or something does. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 2 Chronicles 4:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the removal of something through washing or water.

This is a proper name, identified as “Archyaioi; Arkhiei.” It refers to a named person or group rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, in Ezra 4:9. Because it is a proper name and no verse text or wider context is provided here, its precise referent cannot be explained further from the word alone. Its meaning is therefore best retained as the name “Archyaioi; Arkhiei.”

This word refers to a Hasidean, or to the Hasideans as a group. Used as a noun or adjective, it identifies a person or group by that designation or describes something associated with them. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: twice in 1 Maccabees and once in 2 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun describes a want of discipline—disorderliness, where proper order is lacking. It refers to a condition rather than to a person, object, or specific action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Wisdom 14:26. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain how this condition functions in that passage; the word itself supplies the general idea of disorder and lack of discipline.

This word means “senselessly”: it describes an action done without good sense, sound judgment, or proper consideration. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 31:28. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself points to behavior marked by foolishness or a lack of sensible thought.

Bazes, also rendered Vazes, is a proper name referring to a person. It is not a general description or action word, but an individual name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 14:4. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s role and the significance of the name in that passage cannot be explained from this word alone.

Bakōk, also given as Vakok, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named referent rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Joshua 15:29. The name itself supplies the lexical meaning; identifying exactly whom or what it refers to requires the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective describes speech or conduct that is blasphemous or defamatory—dishonoring what is holy or damaging someone’s name through insulting or slanderous words. It identifies something as offensive, abusive, or injurious in what it says about God or another person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Isaiah, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

This adjective describes something of short performance: it is carried out briefly or does not last long. The word names the limited duration of an action or undertaking rather than expressing a person, object, or feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 15:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This word means “fuller,” a noun identifying a person by that occupation. It is a specific occupational term rather than a general description of an object, action, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: in 2 Kings 18:17, Isaiah 7:3, and Isaiah 36:2. The available wording consistently represents the term as “fuller,” so its central meaning remains the person or occupational role named by that word.

Gōyni, also rendered Guni, is a personal name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it identifies an individual by name. It occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 46:24; without the verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about that person or the surrounding passage. Its basic meaning is therefore its identifying name: Gōyni or Guni.

This Greek LXX noun means “testimony”—a spoken or presented witness to what is known or affirmed. It points to testimony as a declared account or statement, rather than describing the person who gives it. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, appearing once in Genesis and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains a testimony or witness-bearing statement.

“Diaspora” refers to a people living dispersed away from their homeland or gathered community. It is a noun naming this dispersed condition or the people who are dispersed. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs nine times, showing its use across passages about scattering and restoration. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means to strain off, describing the act of filtering something so that unwanted material is separated from what is being kept. It presents straining as a deliberate action rather than merely naming a strained substance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Amos 6:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning is the act of straining or filtering something away.

This word refers to a dynasty or to a dynast—a powerful ruler or member of a ruling house. As a noun, it can designate either the governing family or the person who holds authority within it. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 66 times, showing regular use for people connected with political power and established rule. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on whether the sentence points to the ruling house as a whole or to an individual ruler.

This Greek LXX verb means “exercise control over.” It describes actively directing, restraining, or governing what is placed under someone’s control. As a verb, it points to an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Exodus and four times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding sentence identifies as being controlled.

This Greek LXX verb means “go into”: it describes entering or moving inside a place. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books represented here, with uses ranging from Exodus and 1 Samuel to 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what or whom the subject is entering and the surrounding words.

gl: bind so as to hang from; fasten to
d: bind so as to hang from; fasten to

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to bind something so that it hangs, or to fasten it securely. It describes attaching or securing something, with the resulting position or connection in view. In the LXX corpus, it occurs three times across Joshua, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a passage depends on what is being attached and how the sentence uses the verb.

This noun refers to a person who is a “searcher-out” or “inquisitor”—someone characterized by actively seeking information or examining a matter. It describes the person doing the searching, rather than the search itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Baruch 3:23. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to an investigator or questioner who pursues understanding.

This Greek LXX verb means “break off; snap asunder.” It describes something breaking away or splitting apart suddenly, emphasizing a forceful separation rather than a gentle movement. As a verb, it expresses the action itself. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Job 18:14, so its broader range of use is not demonstrated by repeated occurrences in this corpus. The surrounding verse context would determine exactly what is described there.

This noun means “disadvantage”—a condition, circumstance, or weakness that puts someone at an unfavorable position. It describes something that works against a person or situation rather than helping it. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, in Sirach 19:28 and 2 Maccabees 11:13. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a drawback or unfavorable condition.

This word is the proper name “Elimelek,” functioning as a personal designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It does not provide a general concept such as a virtue, event, or physical thing; its meaning is the name itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:26. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the person’s specific role there, but the word’s ordinary lexical function is simply to identify Elimelek by name.

This word means “spend”. It is a verb describing the act of spending. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Proverbs 23:16. The word’s basic sense remains focused and direct: it expresses spending rather than naming a person, object, or place. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but the lexical idea itself is straightforward. This occurrence belongs to the Greek rendering of the Old Testament, so it should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Greek New Testament term.

“Honourably” describes an action done with respect, dignity, or proper regard for another person. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Numbers 22:17. Its basic sense is therefore focused and specific: it characterizes conduct as honourable. The surrounding verse determines the precise force of that description, but the word itself presents the manner of acting as respectful and worthy of honour.

This verb means to dream—to experience or report dreams during sleep. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Jeremiah 23:25, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word describes the act of dreaming rather than naming a person, object, or place. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means “spring up”: to emerge or grow upward. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes something coming forth rather than remaining hidden or still. It occurs five times, all in Old Testament verses, with four occurrences in Psalms and one in Genesis. Its basic emphasis is the action of appearing or rising into growth. The surrounding words determine whether it refers to a plant, a person, or another thing that comes forth, but the central idea remains emergence and upward growth.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “wake up.” It describes becoming awake or rousing from sleep, and it functions as an action word rather than a name or description. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Judges, 1 Kings, and Job. Its basic sense remains simple: a sleeping person becomes awake. The surrounding verse determines whether the word refers to ordinary sleep or uses waking language in a broader setting.

gl: called upon; called in as allies
d: called upon; called in as allies

e.t: This adjective describes people who are called upon or brought in as allies. It points to those summoned to join, assist, or stand with others, rather than describing an action performed by the person themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, including passages in Numbers, Joshua, and Amos. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains being called in for support or association.

This verb means “glean grapes”—to gather grapes left behind after the main harvesting. It describes the act of collecting what remains in a vineyard rather than performing the primary harvest. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the gathering of leftover grapes.

This noun refers to a mother who has seven children. It is a specific descriptive word, combining the family relationship of motherhood with the number seven. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 16:24. That reference identifies its only recorded occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain what the word contributes in that passage. Its central meaning remains straightforward: a woman described as the mother of seven children.

This noun refers to bodily strength and health—the condition of having physical vigor and soundness. It describes physical well-being rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:19. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context, but its basic meaning remains clear: physical strength joined with healthy bodily condition.

This noun refers to a finding or a piece of good luck—the thing discovered or the fortunate result that comes to someone. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs seven times in Jeremiah and Sirach. Its basic sense can describe something encountered or received as a favorable outcome, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on discovery or good fortune. It names the finding or result rather than describing the action of finding itself.

This noun means “fragrance,” referring to a scent or odor. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 54 times, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its repeated appearance in passages about offerings shows that it can describe the scent associated with sacrificial worship, though the precise force in any verse depends on that passage’s wording and context. The word also appears from Genesis through Baruch, so its basic meaning is not limited to one book or a single ritual setting.

Zara is a personal name used to identify people in the Greek Old Testament. It does not function as a description or action word, but as a proper name preserved in the form “Zara.” This name occurs 14 times across 14 verses in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in genealogical and historical passages from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the person and surrounding passage connected with the name.

This proper name refers to “Ēlam” or “Ilam,” rendered in English as Elam. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears five times, in Ezra and Nehemiah. The name identifies a named entity, but the available word-level information does not specify whether a particular verse is naming a person, a family, or a place. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the surrounding passage rather than to the name itself.

This word means “than.” It is used to connect one person, thing, or statement with another in a comparison, showing that one is being considered in relation to the other. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in 2 Maccabees 14:42 and once in 4 Maccabees 15:16. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding words, but its basic role remains a comparison marker.

This verb means to “fight God”—to oppose God rather than submit to him. It describes resistance directed against God, presenting that resistance as something a person does. In the Greek Old Testament translation corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:19. Its basic sense is focused and direct: it names opposition to God, not merely ordinary disagreement or conflict with another person. Its exact force in that verse is best understood alongside the surrounding wording.

Theree is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 8:35. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one individual in the biblical genealogy. The name itself does not provide enough information to explain that person’s character, role, or significance; those details would require the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek verb means “make noise; in an uproar.” It describes noisy commotion rather than quiet or orderly activity, and it functions as an action word for becoming or being involved in such disturbance. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times across Judges, Daniel, Nahum, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Iediou is a personal name, also rendered Iethiu. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This Greek LXX name occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 9:12 and 1 Chronicles 24:23. The supplied lexical information does not provide a broader definition or an explanation of the name’s origin, so its clear meaning is its function as a personal designation in these genealogical and priestly records.

Iezonias is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. As a name, it does not describe an action, quality, or idea; its role is to designate someone mentioned in the biblical narrative. The name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, across five verses in 2 Kings, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. The particular person or event associated with Iezonias must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

This word identifies the number twenty-one and is also associated with the letter designation “s[h]in.” It functions as a fixed numerical marker rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:161. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, its precise use in that location cannot be described further. Its basic meaning remains a numerical designation: “21; s[h]in.”

This verb means “call” or “invite”: it describes summoning someone, addressing them, or asking them to come. As a verb, it expresses an action directed toward another person or group rather than a thing or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 445 times, showing that calling is a widely used biblical action. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “ground-floor,” describing something located at the lower level of a building. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 6:16. Its basic sense identifies position within a structure rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. The surrounding verse is needed to explain exactly what it describes there, but the word itself points plainly to what is on or near the ground level.

This noun means “legacy”—something passed on or left behind for others. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Genesis 45:7. Its core idea is the lasting portion or benefit preserved for those who come after. Because the word occurs only once and the verse text is not included here, its precise emphasis in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context.

This Greek word means “throw down” or “overthrow.” It is a verb describing the act of forcing something or someone downward, bringing about a fall, or removing a position of strength. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Lamentations and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains decisive downward action—casting down or overturning what was standing.

This adjective means “involved in.” It describes someone or something engaged with a matter, showing participation or connection rather than naming an action by itself. Its exact force depends on what the sentence identifies as the matter involved. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Wisdom 1:4, so its normal meaning is clear even though its broader range cannot be traced through many occurrences.

This verb means to stain or sully—to make something dirty, marked, or defiled. It describes an action rather than a person or object, showing that something has been marred from a clean or acceptable condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 2:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on making something stained or sullied.

This noun means “dice,” referring to the small objects themselves rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears twice: once in Esther and once in Job. Its meaning is straightforward and concrete, identifying dice as physical objects. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how the word functions in either passage, but nothing in its basic sense requires a broader or more symbolic meaning.

This noun refers to a “constellation”—a recognizable pattern of stars in the sky. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs twice, once in 2 Kings 23:5 and once in Job 38:32. Its basic meaning identifies a heavenly star pattern rather than a person, action, or quality. The exact force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word is a proper personal name, given as “Maiēl” or “Mil.” It functions as a name rather than as a description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice in one verse, Genesis 4:18, identifying the same named individual in that genealogical setting. The name’s precise significance is not defined here beyond its role as a personal designation.

This word means “pouch,” referring to a small container used to carry or hold items. It is a noun, so it names the object itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, with most occurrences in Genesis and additional occurrences in Deuteronomy and Micah. Its exact use in any particular sentence depends on what is being placed in the pouch or how the pouch functions in the surrounding passage.

Melchom, also rendered Melkhom, is a proper name. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Jeremiah, at Jeremiah 30:17 and Jeremiah 30:19. The name identifies a specific person, being, or title in those passages, but the word itself does not provide enough information to explain that figure’s role or significance without the surrounding verse text. Its precise reference therefore belongs to the context of each passage rather than to the name alone.

This word means “association”: a connection, relationship, or shared fellowship between people or things. As a noun, it names the bond or participation that joins parties together rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 121:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains one of connection or belonging together.

This verb means to belittle someone or something, or to make it small. It can describe reducing something’s size or lowering its standing, depending on the sentence. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Hosea and once in Sirach. The basic idea remains a movement toward lesser size, importance, or esteem; the surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent.

e.h: A Word for Times As Many As
e.t: This word is an adjective that describes a quality or condition. Its basic sense is “times as many as”. It expresses a comparison of quantity, indicating that one thing is multiplied in relation to another. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalm 67:18, though the verse context is needed to determine exactly what is being compared. This word therefore functions simply as a descriptive term for a specified multiple or amount.

Nanaios, also rendered Naneos, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek LXX corpus and appears once, in 2 Maccabees 1:15. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further. Its basic meaning is therefore the identification of a person named Nanaios or Naneos.

Nebrim, also rendered Nevrim, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise referent is identified by the surrounding passage, but the lexical information preserves the name itself without adding a broader definition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:34. This entry should therefore be understood as a named term, with its particular significance determined from that verse’s context.

This noun refers to a bride or to a daughter-in-law, a woman joined to a family through marriage. Its meaning depends on the relationship being described: it can identify a newly married woman or the wife of someone’s son. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 40 times, including passages in Genesis, Ruth, and Song of Songs. The word therefore covers both family relationship and marital status, rather than naming only one particular stage of marriage.

Xanthikos is a proper name, rendered as “Xanthikos” or “Ksanthikos.” It identifies a person or other named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees 11:30, 11:33, and 11:38. Because the surrounding verse text is not included, these occurrences establish the name’s use but do not identify the person or explain the specific role associated with it in each passage.

Ozia is a proper name used for people identified by that name in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it functions as a personal designation. The name occurs nine times, in passages from 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. Because the available information does not provide the surrounding verse text, the precise identity of each person named Ozia must be determined from the particular passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “frontier”: a boundary marking the limit of a land or territory. It is used especially when Scripture describes the borders of regions, tribes, and nations. The word appears 272 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a regular term for territorial boundaries rather than a rare expression. Its use begins in Genesis and continues through 1 Maccabees, with many occurrences in Joshua, Ezekiel, and Numbers.

This noun means “urine,” referring to the body’s liquid waste. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 2 Kings 18:27 and once in Isaiah 36:12. Its meaning is direct and specific rather than figurative in the lexical information available here. The surrounding wording of each verse would be needed to explain the word’s precise role in those passages.

This Greek LXX verb means “recommend.” It describes a speaker putting forward a course of action or guidance for another person to consider. The word names an action, not a person, object, or abstract quality. Within this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains a recommendation directed toward someone.

This Greek LXX verb means “confine” or “lie around.” It describes something that encloses, surrounds, or lies around another thing. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic idea is positional or enclosing: something is placed around another object, or an object is restricted within surrounding limits. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent in a particular occurrence.

This noun means “mud” or “clay,” referring to soft earth that can be shaped, molded, or used in making something. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for ordinary material from the ground. The word occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Genesis, Job, Isaiah, and other books. Its basic sense can describe the material itself, while the surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on its pliability, lowliness, or use in forming an object.

This verb means “live as a citizen,” describing how a person conducts life as a member of a community. It points to active participation in civic life rather than merely possessing citizenship. In the Greek Old Testament and related Jewish writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages in Esther and the Maccabean books. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea is to live and behave as a citizen within a society.

The word means “purple,” the color. As a noun, it names purple itself or something identified by that color. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 45 times, showing that this is a recurring word rather than a rare designation. Its central meaning remains stable wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines what purple object, material, or feature is being named. The word appears from Exodus through Song of Songs, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books.

This verb means “defend”: to act on behalf of someone or something to protect it against opposition or attack. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears three times, all in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense is an active response of protection, rather than merely observing a danger or expressing support. The surrounding verse determines who is being defended and what kind of opposition is involved.

This Greek Old Testament noun means a “crack” or “fissure”—a split or opening in a solid surface or structure. It names the break itself rather than an action or person. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 4:3 and Ezekiel 27:22. Its basic sense remains physical and concrete; the surrounding verse is needed to determine what object has the crack or fissure and why it is mentioned.

Rōs, also rendered Rhos, is a proper name used for a person or people named in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a designation rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing once in Genesis, once in Jeremiah, and three times in Ezekiel. The available information identifies the name but does not establish a broader ordinary meaning or explain the specific identity referred to in each passage.

Saber, also rendered Saver, is a proper name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 2:48, identifying a person in the genealogical record. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine a further meaning or significance, so it is best understood simply as the individual’s personal name in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “sway” or “rock”—to move, shake, or be made unstable rather than remain firm. It can describe physical movement, but its ordinary sense also allows the picture of something being unsettled or shaken. The word occurs 71 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used across many settings rather than describing only one event. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being shaken and the surrounding context.

Saouia, also written Saoia, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its use as the name of a particular individual or named figure. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:4. The available lexical information preserves these two forms of the name but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or explanation of its name origin.

Senna is a proper name, rendered as “Senna” in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a name rather than as a general description, action, or quality. This word occurs four times in the LXX, across four verses in Numbers, Joshua, and 1 Samuel. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not provide additional meaning or explanation beyond “Senna.” Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “standard,” referring to a banner, ensign, or raised sign used as a visible marker. Its basic sense is something set up so people can recognize a rallying point or direction. In this corpus, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:17. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a clearly displayed standard or signal.

This noun means “dwelling”: a place or state associated with dwelling. It names the idea of inhabiting or having a dwelling, rather than describing an action by itself.
